title: Burst-window fairness controller with token escrow and KV-residency hints
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood's continuous batching runtime must admit and schedule requests across tenants while respecting tail latency SLOs and limited GPU memory for KV caches. Existing approaches have focused on slot-based preemption and tenant-weight quotas, but we still observe bursty tenants starving long-running KV-resident workloads and causing tail-latency violations when GPU memory is transiently overloaded.

Goal:
Design and implement a Burst-window Fairness Controller (BFC) that: 1) preserves short-term burst allowance for interactive tenants, 2) guarantees baseline throughput for KV-warm workloads that hold large residency in GPU memory, and 3) performs low-latency, deterministic preemption when memory pressure threatens SLOs. The controller should integrate with the admission/batcher pipeline and KV residency tracker, emitting signals to the allocator and preemption plane.

High-level approach:
- Token escrow: allocate short-lived burst tokens per tenant that can be spent immediately for low-latency admission. Tokens replenish slowly based on long-term entitlement (tenant weight + committed capacity). Tokens are revocable when KV memory pressure crosses soft thresholds.
- KV-residency hints: extend the KV tracker to expose per-tenant "residency score" (stringified hint) representing working set footprint and hotness decay. The controller uses the score to raise a retention priority for in-flight slices from KV-hot tenants.
- Burst windows: define 250ms sliding windows where token consumption is limited; within each window, the controller enforces a fairness curve that prevents a small set of tenants from monopolizing slice allocations.
- Preemption escrow: when pressure indicates imminent SLO risk (predicted through rolling P99 latency model + memory headroom estimate), the controller initiates an escrowed preemption: it marks low-priority slices for graceful interruption and triggers KV trim candidates (cold items first). If graceful preemption cannot reclaim enough memory within a short timeout, hard revocation applies to non-critical burst tokens.

Architecture changes required:
- Batcher: add admission hook that consults BFC for token availability and ordering hint. The hook returns admission decision + tracing metadata.
- KV tracker: compute residency_score and provide an HTTP/IPC fast path for the BFC to query aggregated hotset info.
- Preemption plane: support two-stage preemption (graceful escrow -> hard revoke) and accept a list of eviction hints (tenant + key groups) from BFC.
- Metrics & observability: new histograms and counters (token_consumed{tenant}, token_replenish_rate, residency_score_gauge, escrowed_preempts, graceful_reclaim_bytes, hard_revokes). Add dashboard rows and alert rules for token exhaustion and repeated hard revokes.

Acceptance criteria:
- Synthetic benchmark: in mixed workload test (50% interactive small prompts, 50% KV-hot long prompts), P99 latency for interactive tenants must not increase by >10% compared to baseline while tail latency for KV-hot tenants remains within 1.5x baseline under 80% GPU memory utilization.
- Memory reclaim latency: graceful-escrow preemption path should reclaim >50% of target bytes within 120ms in 95% of trials.
- No regressions in throughput for dedicated customers participating in reserved capacity tests.
- End-to-end traces must include token lifecycle for >95% of requests.

Non-goals:
- This ticket does not implement new model-quantization strategies or change kernel selection. It focuses solely on runtime admission, token accounting, and preemption orchestration.

Tasks / Subtasks:
- Design doc (this ticket): finalize fairness curve parameters and thresholds. (Aisha)
- KV tracker extension: residency_score API + unit tests. (Marcus)
- BFC core: token escrow accounting, sliding window enforcement, and token revocation logic. (Marcus, Priya Rao)
- Preemption plane changes: graceful escrow handling and eviction hint plumbing. (Ivan Gomez)
- Bench harness: mixed workload generator, memory pressure injector, and custom P99 predictor. (QA - Lena)
- Observability: metrics, dashboards, alerts, and trace annotations. (SRE - Daniel)
- Integration tests / load runs on staging and dedicated clusters. (Team)

Risks and mitigations:
- Incorrect token rates could starve low-priority tenants or under-utilize GPUs. Mitigation: start with conservative replenish rates and A/B test with canary traffic.
- KV residency scoring misestimates hotness: Mitigation: use a decayed access counter + estimated byte footprint; cross-check against realtime cache hit/miss curves.
- Preemption thrash under highly bursty traffic: Mitigation: hysteresis in token revocation and a minimum grace window of 60ms before hard revokes.

Open questions for PM/design review:
- Should burst tokens be transferable across tenant sessions (yes/no)? Current plan: tokens are tenant-scoped, not session-scoped.
- What is the appropriate long-term entitlement model for token replenishment? Options: static tenant weight, cost-based entitlement (dollars consumed), or time-windowed SLA. PM preference requested.

Links and artifacts:
- Design diagram draft (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/CI/Burst+Window+Fairness+Controller
- Prototype PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4567
- Mixed-workload benchmark script: https://internal-scripts/redwood/batches/mixed_burst_test.py

Notes on implementation details:
- Sliding window enforcement will use a fixed-size ring buffer of token consumption events, sharded by tenant to avoid global locks.
- Residency score is a compact string: "r:<decay-counter>:<bytes-est>". BFC will parse these hints and map them into internal float priorities. Keep the API forward-compatible.
- Graceful-escrow preemption will coordinate with frontend request routers to send early 409-ish soft interrupts so clients can retry quickly rather than waiting for hard revokes.

- 2026-02-28: token escrow accounting library completed and unit tested.
- 2026-03-05: integration on staging with observability and first load run.
- 2026-03-12: canary rollout to 10% of host pools; collect metrics for 72 hours.
